Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A Title VII Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case to Survive a Rule 12(b)(6) Motion; She Must Allege Facts That Plausibly Support an Inference of Discrimination.

The district court erred by measuring the complaint against the *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie framework rather than the plausibility standard that governs Rule 12(b)(6). The prima facie case is "an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). Because the framework is a flexible evidentiary tool that may not even apply once a case has evidence of discrimination, requiring a plaintiff to plead each of its elements would impose a heightened pleading burden that Rule 8(a) does not allow. *Id.* at 510–12. Neither *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), nor *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009), displaced that holding. They require that a complaint allege facts that state a plausible claim for relief. *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 570; *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678.

This Court has repeatedly reconciled these principles. In *Coleman v. Maryland Court of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012), the Court explained that *Swierkiewicz* remains good law after *Twombly* and that a plaintiff is not required to plead facts constituting a prima facie case. The complaint must still allege facts that, accepted as true, raise the right to relief above the speculative level and state a plausible claim. *Id.* at 190–91. Likewise, in *McCleary-Evans v. Maryland Department of Transportation, State Highway Administration*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015), the Court confirmed that *Swierkiewicz* survives *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, while recognizing that the elements of a prima facie case can help a court judge whether the facts alleged make discrimination plausible. See also *Goode v. Central Virginia Legal Aid Society, Inc.*, 807 F.3d 619, 626 (4th Cir. 2015) (applying this approach). The inquiry is therefore not whether the plaintiff has pleaded each prima facie element, but whether the complaint, read as a whole, plausibly alleges that the employer acted because of a protected characteristic.

Applying that standard, this Court has reversed dismissals where a plaintiff pleaded concrete facts, even if she did not plead every prima facie element. In *Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648–49 (4th Cir. 2017), the Court reiterated that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case and held that the complaint's factual allegations sufficed to make the claim plausible. In *Bing v. Brivo Systems, LLC*, 959 F.3d 605, 616–17 (4th Cir. 2020), the Court again confirmed that the prima facie elements are not pleading requirements. It asked instead whether the facts alleged supported a reasonable inference of the statutory violation, and it held that they did.

By contrast, *McCleary-Evans* shows what falls short. There the plaintiff alleged little more than that she was qualified, that she was not selected, and that the employer must have been biased, and she pleaded no facts connecting the decision to her protected status. 780 F.3d at 585–86. Her allegations were conclusory, and the complaint itself pointed to non-discriminatory explanations at least as likely as discrimination. *Id.* These principles apply the ordinary rule that courts accept well-pleaded facts as true and draw reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor but do not credit bare legal conclusions. *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 192–93 (4th Cir. 2009); *Nemet Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc.*, 591 F.3d 250, 255–56 (4th Cir. 2009).

The complaint here satisfies that standard. It alleges specific facts, not labels, about Plaintiff's qualifications, the adverse action, the circumstances surrounding the decision, and the treatment of others outside her protected class. These facts, taken together and read in Plaintiff's favor, make discrimination a plausible explanation for the employer's conduct. Plaintiff was not required to anticipate the evidentiary burden-shifting framework or to plead each of its elements. The district court's contrary approach imposed a pleading requirement that *Swierkiewicz* forbids, and its dismissal should be reversed.
